nameStory: The Red-femured Spotted Orbweaver gets its name from the distinctive reddish coloring on its femurs - the first segment of each leg closest to the body. Like other spotted orbweavers, it also displays various spots and markings across its abdomen, giving it a delightfully decorated appearance.
description: This medium-sized spider is a master architect, spinning classic circular webs that glisten with morning dew. The Red-femured Spotted Orbweaver has a rounded abdomen decorated with various spots and patterns, while its most distinctive feature is the reddish coloring on the upper leg segments. These spiders are commonly found around human dwellings, making them one of the more familiar orbweavers you might encounter on porches, gardens, and building exteriors. They typically reach about the size of a nickel when their legs are extended.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Look for the telltale reddish or orange coloring on the femurs (the thick upper leg segments closest to the body) - this warm color stands out against the darker legs

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Rounded, bulbous abdomen with various spots, blotches, or geometric patterns that can range from subtle to quite pronounced

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Classic circular orb web that feels sticky to the touch, typically positioned vertically between structures or plants

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body length reaches about half an inch, with legs extending to roughly nickel-sized overall - substantial enough to notice but not intimidatingly large

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often found on or near buildings, porches, and human structures, where they build their webs in corners, between railings, or spanning doorways

habitat: Red-femured Spotted Orbweavers are particularly fond of human-made environments, earning them their scientific name meaning 'of dwellings.' Look for them around houses, barns, porches, decks, and other buildings where they can anchor their webs between structural elements. They also inhabit gardens, fence lines, and shrubby areas near homes, preferring spots with some shelter and regular insect traffic.

seasonality.spring: Young spiders begin appearing and establishing territories, though they're still quite small and their distinctive leg coloring may not be fully developed yet.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, actively hunting in their webs and displaying their full coloration. This is the best time to spot their characteristic red femurs.
seasonality.fall: Mating season brings increased activity, and egg sacs may be visible. Adults reach their largest size before cold weather arrives.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off, but egg sacs overwinter in protected locations, ready to hatch when warm weather returns.

funFact: These spiders are such fans of human company that their scientific name literally means 'of dwellings' - they've essentially become our architectural roommates, preferring to build their intricate circular webs on our porches and buildings rather than in wild forests.
confusionNotes: The red leg markings are your best clue to separate this from other spotted orbweavers like the common Spotted Orbweaver, which lacks the distinctive reddish femurs. Memory trick: 'Red legs = Red-femured' - it's right there in the name!
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the word 'spotted' fool you - while these spiders do have spots, the 'red-femured' part of their name is actually the more reliable identifying feature, since spot patterns can vary considerably between individuals.
compareHints: Among its Neoscona cousins, the Red-femured Spotted Orbweaver is distinguished by those characteristic reddish femurs that the regular Spotted Orbweaver and Arabesque Orbweaver lack. The Arabesque Orbweaver tends to prefer more natural settings away from buildings, while the Marsh Orbweaver, as its name suggests, sticks to wetland areas rather than porches and homes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Neoscona relatives, the Spotted Orbweaver is most reliably identified by those two white spots on the black underside of the abdomen.
Among its Neoscona relatives, the arabesque orbweaver stands out for its flowing, swirling abdominal patterns rather than distinct spots or geometric shapes.
The Marsh Orbweaver differs from its close relatives like the Spotted Orbweaver and Arabesque Orbweaver primarily by habitat preference - it's the wetland specialist of the group.
